clauses.statement: Over any field and arbitrary finite matrix labels, the vector-relative minimal polynomial is monic, has natural degree equal to the Krylov grade, and is the unique monic annihilator of that degree.

A polynomial annihilates the starting vector exactly when the vector-relative minimal polynomial divides it; the native polynomial-module annihilator ideal is generated by that polynomial, including zero vectors.
The Krylov space has dimension min(q,grade), and its first q powers are independent exactly when q is at most the grade, over an arbitrary scalar field.
The grade-sized Krylov space is invariant under the matrix and every later Krylov space equals it.
The vector-relative minimal polynomial divides the operator minimal polynomial, so the grade is at most its degree and the operator minimal-polynomial degree is at most the ambient dimension.
Grade zero is equivalent to a zero starting vector, and an invertible matrix's inverse image of the starting vector belongs to the grade-sized Krylov space, including empty dimension.
The concrete Frobenius shift-and-negative-coefficients companion of a monic polynomial has that polynomial as both characteristic and minimal polynomial, including the degree-zero polynomial one.

Every finite matrix over any field has a vector realizing its minimal polynomial; full minimal-polynomial degree is equivalent to a full-grade vector and to equality with the characteristic polynomial.

A full-grade vector gives the native basis of successive Krylov powers in which the matrix is its characteristic companion; existence of such a companion basis representation is equivalent to equality of minimal and characteristic polynomials.
For a full-grade vector, every matrix commuting with the operator is the evaluation of a unique polynomial of degree below the dimension, with the zero polynomial in dimension zero.

Over a field where the characteristic polynomial splits, full minimal-polynomial degree is equivalent to a one-dimensional eigenspace for every actual eigenvalue, including repeated eigenvalues and empty dimension.

Field extension preserves the matrix minimal-polynomial degree, so the geometric criterion for a real matrix is correctly equivalent to geometric simplicity of the eigenvalues of its complexification.
Every affine-Krylov iterate has a degree-bounded residual polynomial with constant coefficient one, and every such polynomial has an affine-Krylov representative, for arbitrary real matrices.

For a specified iterate the residual-polynomial converse requires invertibility; the forward error-polynomial identity relative to a supplied exact solution needs no invertibility when the iterate lies in the affine Krylov space.
Residual minimax error is defined by an extended nonnegative uniform supremum over any complex set, decreases with the degree, increases with the domain, is at most one, and is zero on the empty set.

Every compact complex set, including finite and empty sets or sets with invisible coefficient directions, has an attaining real residual polynomial with the advertised degree and constant-coefficient constraints.
On a positive real interval embedded in the complex plane, the residual minimax value is exactly the reciprocal Chebyshev value, including degree zero.

For positive semidefinite Hermitian part, the matrix kernel equals its adjoint kernel and the common kernel of its real and imaginary Hermitian parts; the Hermitian-part rank is no greater than the full rank, including empty dimension.

Equality of matrix and positive-semidefinite Hermitian-part ranks implies identical kernels and complex leading row and column inclusion. Positive definite Hermitian part makes every embedded principal submatrix invertible and gives both inclusion properties.

A positive definite Hermitian part and arbitrary Hermitian imaginary part admit exact relative-diagonal determinant products. Ostrowski-Taussky gives det(H)<=|det(H+iK)| with equality exactly when K=0, including dimension zero.
For dimension at least two, det(H)+|det(K)|<=|det(H+iK)|; for positive dimension, the sharp Fan exponent 2/n gives det(H)^(2/n)+|det(K)|^(2/n)<=|det(H+iK)|^(2/n), including singular K.

The numerical range is the quadratic-form image of the complex Euclidean unit sphere, compact in every finite dimension, includes the complex spectrum, and is contained in the spectral-norm closed disk; empty matrices have empty numerical range.
Affine scalar transformations give the affine image of the numerical range; unitary similarity preserves it; compression by any matrix with orthonormal columns only shrinks it.
In positive dimension the real projection of the numerical range is the interval between the extreme eigenvalues of the Hermitian part.
The numerical range of every finite complex matrix is convex (Toeplitz-Hausdorff), including empty dimension; a Bloch sphere proof establishes the two-dimensional compression case.
For every normal complex matrix the numerical range is exactly the convex hull of its complex spectrum, including repeated eigenvalues and empty dimension.
